A_target.statement:
Let $f: A \to C$ and $g: B \to C$ be [[Definition:Morphism|morphisms]] in a [[Definition:Metacategory|category]] $\mathbf C$.
A [[Definition:Pullback (Category Theory)|pullback]] of $f$ and $g$ is an object $P$ with $p_A: P \to A$, $p_B: P \to B$, $f \circ p_A = g \circ p_B$, which is [[Definition:Terminal Object|terminal]] among such cones over the cospan $A \to C \leftarrow B$.

B_source.statement:
Let $f: C \to A$ and $g: C \to B$ be [[Definition:Morphism|morphisms]].
A [[Definition:Pushout|pushout]] of $f$ and $g$ is an object $Q$ with $q_A: A \to Q$, $q_B: B \to Q$, $q_A \circ f = q_B \circ g$, which is [[Definition:Initial Object|initial]] among such cocones under the span $A \leftarrow C \to B$.

object_map.reformulation: Pass to the opposite category C^op, reversing every morphism, which turns spans into cospans.

validity_conditions: The pushout's universal property is stated purely via arrows and commuting squares, so reversing all arrows yields a valid universal property.
Op is an involution, so the pullback in C equals the pushout in C^op.
proof_plan: Write the [[Definition:Universal Property|universal property]] of the [[Definition:Pushout|pushout]] using only morphisms and commuting squares.

Reverse every morphism, passing to $\mathbf C^{\text {op} }$.
The span becomes a cospan, and the cocone becomes a cone.
Initial becomes terminal, and the reversed property is the definition of the [[Definition:Pullback (Category Theory)|pullback]].

Hence a pullback in $\mathbf C$ is a pushout in $\mathbf C^{\text {op} }$.
{{qed}}
